lesson.title: Vestments, incense, and the sign of the cross

readings.title: Priestly vestments
readings.locator: The Symbolism of the Church, p.xxxv
readings.text: Priests. The Priest's stikhár, or cassock (Podríznik), has close sleeves. His Stole (Epitrakhil) consists of a long piece of stuff like the Deacon's, but broader than the latter, which passes round his neck, is joined in front for its entire length, and falls low upon his cassock. It typifies the consecrating grace of the Priesthood. The Priest, like the Deacon, can celebrate no Office without his Stole. In it, without the Chasuble, he celebrates the less solemn Offices: Lesser Vespers, ordinary Compline, Lauds (Polunótchnitza), the Hours (if the Gospel be not appointed to be read in them); also various Prayer-services in private dwellings, such as that at the birth of a child, and the like.

readings.title: Incense
readings.locator: The Symbolism of the Church, p.xxxiii
readings.text: The Holy Images (Ikóni), the Holy Things, and the people who are present at the divine service, are honoured with incense. The censing before the Holy Door signifies the desire of the worshippers that their prayers shall be borne up to the throne of God, as the incense from the censer is wafted heavenward; and that their petitions shall be well-pleasing to God like fragrant incense. The censing of the people is symbolical of the grace of the Holy Spirit, which is shed abroad everywhere, upon all men. The censer (Kadílo) represents the Divine Ember, even Christ.

overview.text: Vestments are the garments associated with liturgical ministry, and incense is used in censing people and sacred things. These readings introduce their meaning in Hapgood’s explanation, with further OCA resources on vestments and the sign of the cross.

paragraphs.text: The epitrachelion is the priest’s stole, worn around the neck and hanging down the front. Hapgood relates it to the grace of priestly ministry and describes its use in the services of her edition. The word identifies a particular garment, not every piece of a priest’s clothing.

readings.title: What does the commentary say about incense?

paragraphs.text: Hapgood relates rising incense to prayer and describes censing of icons, sacred things and the assembled people. She interprets the censing of people through the grace of the Holy Spirit. These are the explanations attached to this historical source, rather than newly invented meanings for the objects.

readings.title: What does the sign of the cross express?

paragraphs.text: The linked OCA article connects the sign of the cross with the confession of the Trinity and with Christ’s saving cross. It explains a bodily gesture as an expression of Christian belief and commitment; the lesson does not add a new ritual procedure.
